title: Effectiveness of Treatment Elements of Behavioral Parent Training (BPT) for Families of Children with ADHD
summary:
Behavioral parent training (BPT) is an established and effective intervention for children with ADHD. It supports parents in developing consistent, structured, and responsive strategies to manage their child’s behavior in everyday situations. While BPT is widely used, the specific content of these programs can vary – some focus more on psychoeducation, while others emphasize practical strategies like positive reinforcement or managing challenging behavior.
Recent findings suggest that certain behavioral techniques may be more effective in improving parenting outcomes than others. However, these components have rarely been studied separately, and little is known about how they influence child outcomes directly.
Moreover, many BPT programs do not account for whether parents themselves experience ADHD symptoms, which can impact how well they apply the strategies taught. Difficulties in emotion regulation may play a key role here, yet this is rarely addressed in standard programs.
Given rising demand for mental health services and limited clinical resources, group-based BPT offers a promising and efficient alternative to individual therapy. Still, there is a lack of clear evidence on which components of BPT are most effective and for whom – particularly with regard to improvements in child behavior and the family climate.
This randomized microtrial investigates the effects of two specific BPT elements – token economy and parental emotion regulation – on family climate and ADHD symptoms in children with ADHD. The findings aim to support the development of more targeted and resource-sensitive treatment approaches.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
• Child age 6;00 – 13;11 years of age
• Child diagnosis of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) (assessed with the structured clinical parent interview Kinder-DIPS)
• IQ > 70 (clinical impression)
• Child is insured in a statutory health insurance 
• Informed consent of both parents / guardians and an assent of the child
Exclusion criteria:
• Presence of a contraindication for outpatient parent training (e.g., need for more intensive treatment) (clinical impression based on structured clinical parent interview Kinder-DIPS)
• current inpatient or outpatient psychotherapy for the child
